summary: Caisson lighthouse on a shoal about 16 miles off Sabine Pass, Texas: lit in 1906, unattended from 1922, its iron tower taken down from 2002.

lens.where: Museum of the Gulf Coast, Port Arthur

structures.note: Caisson foundation, filled with concrete, with cisterns at its top (LighthouseFriends)
Cast-iron tower, 72 feet from base of structure to lantern center (US Lighthouse Society). Upper part dismantled in 2002; top section and lantern at Lions Park, Sabine Pass
55-foot steel skeleton tower on the caisson's main deck (Coast Guard notice of 2001, as quoted by LighthouseFriends). Completion and lighting are not confirmed in the sources

access.note: Not open to the public (US Lighthouse Society). Offshore; reached only by boat (LighthouseFriends). The Coast Guard issued the 2001 notice for the reconfiguration.

events.note: Congressman William H. Crain proposes a lightship for the bank; the district lighthouse engineer in New Orleans sees no need (LighthouseFriends)
Act of March 3, 1899 authorizes a light and fog signal, cost not exceeding $50,000; no appropriation made
Act of June 6, 1900 appropriates $40,000 for the light and fog signal
Act of March 3, 1901 appropriates a further $40,000 to satisfy the contract
Caisson towed out June 23, 1904, sunk to its target depth on July 21, and completed in August 1904
Storm of October 7, 1905 strikes the construction site; the crew sit out the night in the open caisson
Third-order Fresnel lens first exhibited on March 15, 1906
Daboll trumpet fog signal, run by two five-horsepower oil engines
Hurricane of August 16 and 17, 1915 damages the gallery, roof and boats; the keepers keep the light until forced off for lack of water on August 19
Relit August 23, 1915 after the keepers returned
Principal keeper Albert B. Modawell adrift in a small boat for over 24 hours; found by the Coast Guard cutter Comanche (LighthouseFriends)
Iron shell plates, davits and footplates installed, closing in the veranda (repairs after the 1915 hurricane)
Hurricane of September 13 to 14, 1919; Ericksen and Hansen commended for maintaining the light
Another powerful hurricane strikes the station (LighthouseFriends)
Assistant keeper picked up at sea by the Norwegian tanker Belridge after two and a half days adrift in a disabled motorboat (LighthouseFriends)
Oil-vapor light replaced by an acetylene cluster of three burners showing a white flash every five seconds (2-second flash, 3-second eclipse)
Acetylene light activated August 22, 1922 and the last resident keepers left (LighthouseFriends); the Bulletin's 1922 list records the oil-to-acetylene change. The record gives 1923
Lighthouse Service reports the station converted to an unattended acetylene installation; saving about $5,400 a year
Light not visible on a clear night (19 April 1924); a small hawk in the lantern room had put out the pilot flames
Light source converted to a 150-watt lamp run from a 32-volt battery
Fresnel lens removed from the lantern room; the tower converted to solar power
Coast Guard notice of March 1, 2001 for demolition above the caisson and a new 55-foot steel skeleton tower (as LighthouseFriends quotes it)
Original tower above the caisson replaced by a steel skeleton tower; work began late January 2002
Top section of the tower and the lantern dismantled and taken ashore; on display at Lions Park, Sabine Pass
Discontinued (US Lighthouse Society)

corrections.why: The US Lighthouse Society gives 29 deg 28.3 min N, 93 deg 43.4 min W for Sabine Bank. LighthouseFriends places the light about fifteen miles out from the Sabine River, and the 1923 Bulletin says about 16 miles off the entrance to Sabine Pass. The recorded point lies about 35 km away, further south-east. LighthouseFriends' own pin (29.73482, -93.89392) is at the river mouth and conflicts with its text; see notes.

LighthouseFriends says an acetylene light was activated on August 22, 1922 and the last resident keepers left; the Lighthouse Service Bulletin's 1922 list records the oil-to-acetylene change. The 1923 date in the record comes from a 1923 report of the same change.

notes_for_editor: Status: the record has the light inactive, deactivated in 2001 (Wikidata) and discontinued in 2002 (US Lighthouse Society). Wikipedia (not cited) says the light is still active as an automated beacon on a skeleton tower; the US Coast Guard Historian's page (its archived copy was not reachable, and only its search excerpt was seen) gives 'replaced with a skeleton tower with automated beacon'. Whether the new beacon shows a light is not settled by the sources read; check the Coast Guard Light List (record's LLNR 4-22540) before publication, and set the status accordingly. Characteristic: the record's 'Iso R 6s' is not supported by any source read; the 1923 Bulletin describes a white flash every five seconds on the acetylene light (event dated 1922). Location: the record's point (29.28, -93.43) is about 35 km from the US Lighthouse Society's point; the roster tool matched by name only and warned of the distance. The roster's dates, LighthouseFriends' keepers and the Bulletins agree with the USLHS place, so the USLHS roster is taken as this light's. LighthouseFriends' own coordinates (29.73482, -93.89392) sit at the river mouth and contradict its text (fifteen miles out); treat that pin as unreliable. Tower height: the US Lighthouse Society gives 72 feet from base of structure to lantern center, LighthouseFriends gives 50 feet from the top of the caisson to the ventilator ball. Both are used. Dates of construction contracts (1903 bids, the 1904 caisson, the 1905 storm, the 1906 first light) rest on LighthouseFriends and the Lighthouse Board volumes that are not in the corpus (1903 to 1905 are not covered), so they are checked only where a source is cited. Keepers: 101 stints from the US Lighthouse Society roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory, per the roster tool); 91 of 101 last a year or less. Confirm each name in a primary record before publication. Two roster lines have only one date ('-1914', 'at least 1921-'). The unnamed 1920 assistant in LighthouseFriends ('C.H. Peoples') is not matched to the roster (the roster has Guy H. Peeples, second assistant, 1920), so the story does not name him. The 1915 Bulletin index prints 'George W. Gauthier'; the story follows the roster and the Bulletin's text (Joseph W. Gauthier). Bulletins of 1915, 1922 and 1923 print 'Sabine Bank, La.' or 'Light Station, La.'; the station is in Texas (LighthouseFriends, the US Lighthouse Society, and the Commissioner's lists print 'Tex.'). Ownership: the Coast Guard issued the 2001 notice; no source read states who owns the caisson, so the story does not claim it. Newspapers: Chronicling America gave one Texas page (San Antonio Daily Light, 11 July 1904) that mentions the lighthouse tender Ivy heading for the Sabine banks, not used; the search for the 1915 and 1919 hurricanes and the caisson returned nothing usable. Putnam's 1917 history is in the general series but describes this station, so the story cites it as a source for station facts, not as general context. LighthouseFriends' visitor details (the Museum of the Gulf Coast's hours) may change; check before publication. The Lighthouse Society's record names the museum the Gulf Coast Maritime Museum; the story uses LighthouseFriends's name and gives the record's name once. The story does not say whether the 2002 steel tower was completed or lit, because the sources read do not say; a Coast Guard Light List check would settle it.
